To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) at 160 K more residues are affected than at 100K, and the X-ray-induced relative B-factor increase is correlated to the distance from solvent channels, (ii) at 160K, more residue types are damaged, and the X-rays induce a relative increase in atomic B-factor that is correlated to the proximity to solvent channels.
radiation damage is higher at 160 than at 100K, and that at 160K damage is more likely to occur near solvent channels.
radiation damage in thermolysin crystals occurs more readily at 160 K compared to 100 K and that radiation damage is correlated with the distance to the nearest solvent channels in the crystal.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the influence of the crystallographic temperature on the radiation damage.
the global sensitivity of the protein crystal to X-rays at 160 and 100 K.
the influence of the temperature on radiation damage and the resulting effect on the quality of diffraction data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
at 160 K more types of radiation damage are induced, but that the overall damage level is lower than at 100 and that the damage pattern is more random.
the temperature-dependence of the radiation damage in macro-molecular crystallography depends strongly on the protein crystal under study.
the temperature dependence of radiation damage is complex and depends on the crystal structure and the X-ray wavelength.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the radiation sensitivity of thermolysins is lower at 100 K than at 160 K, which can be explained by the lower thermal energy and mobility of the protein at 100 K, which makes the protein less prone to attack by reactive radicals.
at 160 K the radiation-induced structural changes are more pronounced and the crystal is less stable than at 100K.
the radiation damage at 160 K is more severe than at 100, but that it is not as severe as expected from the higher temperature.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the temperature dependence of radiation damage is not a straightforward issue.
data collection at 100 K is still the best way to minimize radiation damage in macrromolecular crystallography.
data collection at 160 K is not recommended for macromolecular crystallography, unless the protein under study is known to be radiation sensitive at 100 K.
